summaries.example: A tornado is made from tiny bits of matter, such as air and dust. Still, we can study what tornadoes do—spin, move, and change—without knowing every detail about tiny particles. The tornado depends on its parts, but its organized pattern gives it features we describe at a larger level.
summaries.summary: Emergent properties are features of organized wholes that depend on smaller parts but are not simply features of those parts one by one. A tornado, an ant colony, or a living thing is built from smaller components. Yet these wholes can have recognizable patterns and behaviors that scientists study at their own level. The entry calls this combination dependence and autonomy. Some philosophers think larger-level features are fully fixed by physical facts, although they may be difficult to predict or explain from the bottom up. This is often called weak emergence. Others think some larger-level features have genuinely new powers or laws. This is called strong emergence. The entry explains several ways to understand dependence, including necessary connection, being built by lower-level processes, and being caused by them. It also describes disagreements about whether higher-level causes would create a problem if physical causes are already sufficient.
key_ideas: Many things are made of smaller parts but also have patterns that belong to the whole.
Emergence joins two ideas: dependence on parts and some independence in how the whole behaves.
A tornado can be studied as a tornado even though it is made from air, dust, and other tiny things.
Philosophers disagree about how strongly a whole can affect or differ from its parts.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea of emergence helps us think about how different sciences fit together. Physics studies very small or basic processes, while biology, psychology, and other sciences study organized systems. Emergence asks whether these larger sciences describe real features of the world, or only convenient ways of talking about tiny physical events. It also raises questions about living things, minds, and complex systems without assuming that one answer has already won.

important_terms.definition: A feature or behavior that appears in an organized whole but is not found in the same way in each separate part.
The idea that a whole or its features rely on what its smaller parts are like and how they are arranged.
The idea that a larger system has its own patterns or behaviors, so we can study it at its own level.
The view that everything in nature is fully made and explained by basic physical parts.

questions_to_think_about: Can a group have a feature that none of its members has alone?
Does understanding every tiny part always explain what the whole system does?
How can a whole depend on its parts while still being worth studying on its own?

summaries.example: Consider a mental state such as pain. A physicalist functionalist might say that pain is realized by some lower-level physical process that responds to injury and guides behavior, while allowing that different physical processes could realize pain in different organisms. A strong emergentist might instead argue that conscious experience involves a fundamentally new power not possessed by the neural base. The example shows why dependence and autonomy can be interpreted in competing ways.
summaries.summary: The entry presents ontological emergence as a proposed middle position between substance dualism and reductionism. Emergent entities and features are not free-floating: they depend on lower-level physical entities and configurations. At the same time, they may display autonomy, meaning that their organization, properties, laws, or causal patterns are not merely simple sums of the properties of their components. Dependence can be expressed as supervenience, functional realization, or a nomological or causal relation. Autonomy can be associated with non-aggregative behavior, multiple realizability, and distinctive efficacy. Weak emergence preserves physicalism and causal closure. It treats higher-level entities—such as organisms or mental states—as real and explanatorily useful while denying that they introduce fundamentally new physical powers. Several strategies support this view, including token identity with type non-identity, realization, mechanistic organization, and explanatory incompressibility in complex systems. Strong emergence goes further. It allows higher-level properties or organized structures to possess novel causal powers or laws, or for components to acquire new powers when configured in wholes. Critics question whether this is coherent, whether it has empirical support, and whether its supposedly new powers collapse into powers already present at the lower level. The entry surveys possible cases, including consciousness, chemistry, quantum phenomena, and spacetime, while emphasizing that their status remains disputed.
key_ideas: Emergence is defined by a tension between dependence on micro-level configurations and autonomy at a higher level.
Dependence may be understood through modal necessity, functional realization, or nomological and causal relations.
Autonomy may involve non-aggregative organization, multiple realizability, or distinctive causal relevance.
Weak emergence accepts physicalism and usually explains higher-level powers as inherited from, or realized by, lower-level powers.
Strong emergence rejects at least some physicalist commitments by proposing fundamentally novel powers, laws, or transformations.
A major challenge for weak emergence is whether higher-level causes become causally excluded or overdetermined by lower-level causes.
summaries.why_it_matters: Emergence concerns the structure of scientific explanation and the relation among levels of reality. If biological, psychological, or chemical properties are real but depend on physical organization, then the sciences may be connected without one simply replacing all the others. The debate also affects how we understand consciousness, agency, complex systems, and the possibility of downward causation. It is not settled by definitions alone: proposed accounts must be assessed in light of metaphysical arguments and empirical theories.

important_terms.definition: A feature of a complex whole that depends on lower-level features while remaining distinct from them in some philosophically important respect.
A relation in which one set of properties cannot differ without a corresponding difference in another set; the source discusses modal versions of this relation.
The claim that a higher-level state is implemented by some lower-level physical process playing the relevant causal or functional role.
The thesis that all natural phenomena are wholly constituted and metaphysically determined by fundamental physical phenomena.
The claim that some higher-level features possess fundamentally novel causal powers, forces, or laws.
A form of emergence compatible with physicalism and physical causal closure, often involving higher-level explanatory or causal autonomy without new fundamental powers.
The thesis that every fundamental physical effect has a purely fundamental physical cause.
The ability of one kind of higher-level property or process to be produced by different lower-level physical realizations.

questions_to_think_about: Is explanatory irreducibility enough for genuine ontological emergence, or must emergent properties have new powers?
Can a higher-level cause be causally relevant if every physical effect already has a lower-level physical cause?
Does multiple realizability show that a higher-level property is autonomous, or only that it is described at a broader level?
Would strong emergence make the natural world less unified, or could new laws be discovered as they have been in science before?
Should the reality of special-science entities depend on whether a complete physics could describe them?

summaries.example: Think about an ant colony. One ant follows simple local interactions, but the colony can form trails, gather food, and respond to danger. These colony patterns depend on what the ants do, yet no single ant has the colony’s organized behavior. One philosopher might call this weak emergence if the pattern is fully fixed by the ants and their environment. Another might ask whether the colony has a more independent kind of causal power.
summaries.summary: Emergent properties belong to systems made from smaller components, such as organisms, ant colonies, or mental systems. The central idea combines dependence and autonomy. Dependence means that the larger system and its features rely on the parts and their arrangement. Autonomy means that the system has patterns, properties, or behaviors that are not simply the parts listed separately or added together. Philosophers describe dependence in several ways. A higher-level feature might necessarily accompany a lower-level base, be realized by a lower-level process, or be connected to it through laws or causes. They also describe autonomy in different ways. Group behavior may be non-aggregative, a function may have many possible physical realizations, and a higher-level description may identify important causes even when a lower-level description is also true. Weak emergence keeps physicalism: everything still depends on fundamental physical reality, and no new fundamental physical power is required. Strong emergence says that some higher-level features may have new powers or laws. Critics of weak emergence worry about parsimony and causal overdetermination: if physical causes are already enough, what work is left for higher-level causes? Critics of strong emergence worry that it may be unexplained or that its new powers are not really new. The entry treats these as open philosophical disputes rather than settled conclusions.
key_ideas: A system can depend completely on its parts while still having patterns that are best described at the system level.
Emergence is not just about surprise; it is a philosophical claim about how higher-level features relate to lower-level reality.
Weak emergentists accept higher-level science while keeping a physicalist picture of nature.
Strong emergentists think some higher-level features may add new causal powers or laws.
Philosophers debate whether higher-level causes are genuinely causal or are excluded by lower-level physical causes.
summaries.why_it_matters: Emergence gives us a way to ask how the sciences connect. Biology may study organisms, psychology may study minds, and physics may study basic physical processes. The question is whether higher-level descriptions reveal real features of nature or are only useful shortcuts. Thinking about emergence also helps explain why a system can be dependent on its parts without being scientifically interchangeable with a list of those parts.

important_terms.definition: A property of an organized whole that depends on its components but may not be found in any component separately.
The relationship between a larger system or feature and the smaller parts or processes on which it relies.
A kind of independence: the whole has its own patterns, categories, or effects that are not simple additions of the parts.
A relation in which changes in one level require corresponding changes at another level, under a relevant kind of necessity.
The view that higher-level properties are carried out by lower-level processes that perform the needed causal role.
Emergence that remains compatible with physicalism and the idea that physical effects have physical causes.
Emergence involving genuinely new powers or laws at a higher level, beyond what weak emergence allows.
The claim that higher-level properties can be produced by more than one different lower-level arrangement.

questions_to_think_about: If a colony’s behavior comes from its ants, is the colony doing anything new?
Can something be real even if it is fully determined by smaller parts?
Does being hard to predict show that a feature is emergent, or only that the system is complicated?
Would different physical arrangements that produce the same function support the idea of multiple realizability?
What evidence would be needed to support strong emergence?
